\chapter{Head and Hand}
\label{ch:ar-head-and-hand}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the head and the hand in Arabic.}

Say yad, set it against its near-identical Hebrew twin, and contrast how much further raʾs drifted.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{رأس}]{\ar{رأس} (raʾs) — the head}

\label{lesson:AR-C11-ras}



\begin{quote}
One more ancient Semitic root — and a word still hard at work in modern political vocabulary, the same way Latin's \emph{caput} is in English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\ar{رأس}} (\emph{raʾs}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{head}\textquotedblright{} — an ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{ראש}} (\emph{rosh}), the very word inside \textbf{Rosh Hashanah}, \textquotedblleft{}head of the year.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{culture}
Arabic builds \textbf{\ar{رئيس}} (\emph{raʾīs}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{president, chief, head {[}of an organization{]}},\textquotedblright{} directly on this same root — literally \textquotedblleft{}the one who is the head.\textquotedblright{} That's exactly the move English makes with Latin \emph{caput}: \textbf{captain} (\textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} of a unit), \textbf{capital} (\textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} city). Different language families, the same very human idea — the person or place \textquotedblleft{}at the head\textquotedblright{} is the one in charge.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}raʾs\textquotedblright{} — head
  \item \textquotedblleft{}raʾīs\textquotedblright{} — president, literally \textquotedblleft{}the head {[}one{]}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Hebrew cousin — \textquotedblleft{}raʾs / rosh\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{رأس}} mean, and what's its Hebrew cousin? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Head\textquotedblright{}} — cousin of \textbf{rosh}, as in Rosh Hashanah.) What word is built on it for \textquotedblleft{}president,\textquotedblright{} and what does it literally mean? (\textbf{\ar{رئيس}} \emph{raʾīs}, \textquotedblleft{}the head {[}one{]}\textquotedblright{} — the same \textquotedblleft{}head = leader\textquotedblright{} idea as English \emph{captain/capital} from Latin \emph{caput}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{يد}]{\ar{يد} (yad) — the hand}

\label{lesson:AR-C11-yad}



\begin{quote}
Some words wear their age lightly — worn down, reshaped, disguised. This one hasn't changed much at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\ar{يد}} (\emph{yad}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hand}\textquotedblright{} — a short, ancient Semitic root. Its Hebrew cousin is spelled and pronounced almost \textbf{identically}: \textbf{\he{יד}} (\emph{yad}). Where \emph{raʾs/rosh} show a family resemblance, \emph{yad/yad} is closer to twins — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the whole Semitic family.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}yad\textquotedblright{} — hand
  \item the Hebrew twin — \textquotedblleft{}yad\textquotedblright{} — almost the same word
  \item contrast — \textquotedblleft{}raʾs/rosh\textquotedblright{} changed more than \textquotedblleft{}yad/yad\textquotedblright{} did
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{يد}} mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Hand.\textquotedblright{}}) How does it compare to its Hebrew cousin? (\textbf{Nearly identical} — both \emph{yad} — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the Semitic family.)
\end{tcolorbox}
